LONDON, England (CNN) -- A portrait painted 400 years ago and kept anonymously in an Irish home for much of the time since is now believed to be the only painting of William Shakespeare created during his lifetime. The portrait of William Shakespeare is thought to be the "only" portrait painted during his lifetime. The image reveals a wealthy Shakespeare of high social status, contradicting the popular view of a struggling playwright of humble status, according to Stanley Wells, a professor who chairs London's Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. Wells, a distinguished Shakespeare scholar, arranged for three years of research and scientific testing which confirmed it was painted around 1610, when Shakespeare would have been 46 years old. "A rather young looking 46, it has to be said," Wells said. Shakespeare died in 1616. The Cobbe portrait -- named after the Irish family that owns the painting -- shows Shakespeare with rosy cheeks, a full head of hair, and a reddish brown beard. The most common portrait of Shakespeare is a gray image showing a bald Bard with a small mustache and beard, and bags under his eyes. The identity of the man in the portrait was lost over the centuries -- until Alec Cobbe saw a portrait from Washington's Folger Shakespeare Library. That painting, which fell into disfavor as a Shakespeare portrait about 70 years ago, turned out to be one of four copies of Cobbe's portrait. The portrait "shows a man wearing expensive costuming, including a very beautifully painted ruff of Italian lacework which would have been very expensive," Wells said. "It establishes, for me, that Shakespeare in his later years was a rather wealthy, a rather well affluent member of aristocratic circles in the society of his time," Wells said. "There's been too much of a tendency to believe that Shakespeare, being the son of a glover, coming for a small town in the middle of England, that he necessarily retained a rather humble status throughout his life." Wells reads even more into what he sees in Shakespeare's newly-found face. "I think it's plausible as a portrait as a good listener, of somebody who would have been capable of writing the plays, clearly the face of a man of high intelligence," he said. "It's the face of a man, I think, who betrays a good deal of wisdom in his features. But, of course, as somebody (King Duncan) says in Shakespeare's story Macbeth, 'there's no art to find the mind's construction in the face.'" It should be noted that Shakespeare's King Duncan paid a price for judging Macbeth to have the face of an honorable man. Macbeth later murdered the king. The public can read Shakespeare's face from the original painting at Shakespeare Birthplace Trust in Stratford-upon-Avon where it goes on display for several months starting April 23. The portrait then returns to the Cobbe family, which inherited it when an ancestor married England's Earl of Southampton -- a friend of Shakespeare who likely commissioned its painting.

LONDON, England (CNN) — A portrait painted 400 years ago—and kept anonymously in an Irish home for much of the intervening period—is now believed to be the only portrait of William Shakespeare created during his lifetime.

According to Stanley Wells, a distinguished Shakespeare scholar and chairman of London’s Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, the portrait depicts a wealthy Shakespeare of high social standing, challenging the popular image of a struggling playwright from humble origins.

Wells arranged three years of research and scientific testing, which confirmed that the portrait was painted around 1610, when Shakespeare would have been 46 years old.

“A rather young-looking 46, it has to be said,” Wells remarked.

Shakespeare died in 1616.

The Cobbe portrait—named after the Irish family that owns it—shows Shakespeare with rosy cheeks, a full head of hair, and a reddish-brown beard. By contrast, the most familiar portrait of Shakespeare is a gray image depicting a balding Bard with a small mustache and beard and bags beneath his eyes.

The identity of the man in the Cobbe portrait was lost over the centuries, until Alec Cobbe saw a portrait from Washington’s Folger Shakespeare Library. That painting, which fell out of favor as a portrait of Shakespeare about 70 years ago, proved to be one of four copies of the Cobbe portrait.

The portrait “shows a man wearing expensive clothing, including a very beautifully painted ruff of Italian lacework, which would have been very expensive,” Wells said.

“It establishes, for me, that Shakespeare in his later years was a rather wealthy, rather affluent member of aristocratic circles in the society of his time,” he added. “There’s been too much of a tendency to believe that Shakespeare, being the son of a glover and coming from a small town in the middle of England, necessarily retained a rather humble status throughout his life.”

Wells reads even more into Shakespeare’s newly discovered face.

“I think it’s plausible as a portrait of a good listener, of somebody who would have been capable of writing the plays—clearly the face of a man of high intelligence,” he said. “It’s the face of a man, I think, who betrays a good deal of wisdom in his features. But, of course, as somebody—King Duncan—says in Shakespeare’s tragedy *Macbeth*, ‘There’s no art to find the mind’s construction in the face.’”

It should be noted that Shakespeare’s King Duncan paid a price for judging Macbeth to have the face of an honorable man: Macbeth later murdered the king.

The public will be able to examine Shakespeare’s face in the original painting at the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust in Stratford-upon-Avon, where it will be displayed for several months beginning April 23.

The portrait will then return to the Cobbe family, which inherited it after an ancestor married into the family of England’s Earl of Southampton—a friend of Shakespeare who likely commissioned the painting.

Wells organized three years of scientific analysis and historical investigation. The work dated the painting to approximately 1610, when Shakespeare was 46—although Wells observed that the subject appears fairly youthful for that age. Shakespeare died six years later, in 1616.

This appearance differs sharply from the best-known image of the Bard, which portrays him in gray tones as bald, with a slight mustache and beard and visible bags beneath his eyes.

Over time, knowledge of the sitter’s identity disappeared. The connection was rediscovered only after Alec Cobbe noticed another portrait at the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington. That picture had ceased to be widely accepted as an authentic Shakespeare likeness roughly 70 years earlier, but researchers determined that it was one of four copies of the Cobbe painting.

Wells noted that the sitter is dressed in costly clothing, including an intricately rendered ruff made from Italian lace, an item that would have been extremely expensive. In his view, such details indicate that Shakespeare had become wealthy in his later life and moved within the aristocratic circles of his era.

Wells argued that too many people have assumed Shakespeare must have remained socially humble because he was a glove maker’s son from a small town in central England. The portrait, he believes, suggests otherwise.

He also sees the face as that of an attentive listener and a highly intelligent person—someone convincingly capable of writing Shakespeare’s plays. To Wells, the sitter’s features also convey considerable wisdom. He nevertheless acknowledged the danger of drawing conclusions about character from appearance, referring to King Duncan’s observation in *Macbeth* that a person’s thoughts cannot be reliably determined from his face.

Duncan himself suffered the consequences of such a judgment: he believed Macbeth looked honorable, only to be murdered by him later.

# Portrait may offer rare glimpse of Shakespeare from life

**LONDON, England —** A painting that spent centuries hanging in an Irish country house may be the only surviving portrait of William Shakespeare painted during the playwright’s lifetime, researchers announced Monday.

The portrait, known as the Cobbe portrait, shows a dark-haired man with a high forehead, trimmed beard and elaborate white collar. Experts supporting the identification believe it was painted around 1610, when Shakespeare was about 46 — six years before his death.

If authentic, the image could provide an unusually direct look at the author of “Hamlet,” “Macbeth” and “Romeo and Juliet.”

“This is a remarkable claim, and one supported by a substantial body of evidence,” said Stanley Wells, a leading Shakespeare scholar and chairman of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust.

The painting belongs to art restorer Alec Cobbe, whose family had kept it for generations without recognizing the sitter as Shakespeare. Cobbe began investigating after seeing an exhibition of Shakespeare portraits in London in 2006 and noticing similarities between his family’s painting and an image long associated with the dramatist.

Scientific examination dated the wooden panel and pigments to the early 17th century. Researchers also traced the portrait’s ownership to a family with connections to Henry Wriothesley, the 3rd Earl of Southampton, Shakespeare’s patron and the dedicatee of two of his narrative poems.

The painting appears to have served as the source for several later copies, including one associated with the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington. Supporters say those versions strengthen the case that the Cobbe portrait is the original.

The sitter is shown wearing costly clothing, suggesting a man of status and success. An inscription above his head, taken from the Roman poet Horace, has been interpreted as a warning about the uncertain alliances of powerful men.

Not everyone is convinced.

Identifying portraits from the period is notoriously difficult, and no surviving document explicitly names Shakespeare as the sitter. Some art historians have argued that the man could be another prominent Jacobean figure, including the poet and courtier Sir Thomas Overbury.

Only two images of Shakespeare are widely accepted as having strong claims to authenticity: the engraving by Martin Droeshout that appeared in the 1623 First Folio and the funerary monument in Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon. Both were created after Shakespeare’s death in 1616, though people who knew him are believed to have approved them.

The Cobbe portrait’s significance therefore rests on its proposed date. If the identification is correct, Shakespeare may have sat for it himself.

The portrait was presented to the public by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust in Stratford-upon-Avon as part of an exhibition examining the evidence behind the claim.

For scholars accustomed to searching Shakespeare’s plays and poems for traces of the man behind them, the painting offers a tantalizing possibility: not merely an imagined likeness, but the face his contemporaries may actually have seen.

## Science and a Folger Copy Put the Cobbe Portrait at the Center of a Shakespeare Mystery

**STRATFORD-UPON-AVON, England —** A portrait preserved for centuries in an Anglo-Irish family collection has emerged as one of the most closely studied candidates for a lifetime likeness of William Shakespeare, after scientific examination and comparisons with related paintings—including a copy at the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington—suggested that it was created around 1610 and served as the model for later images identified as the playwright.

Known as the **Cobbe portrait**, the painting shows a fashionably dressed man with a high forehead, a pointed beard and an elaborate lace collar. Its identification as Shakespeare was announced in 2009 by Shakespeare scholar Stanley Wells and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. If their conclusion is correct, the portrait was painted about six years before Shakespeare’s death in 1616 and may be the only surviving image of him made from life whose original form remains substantially intact.

The claim is not universally accepted. Some specialists have proposed that the sitter was another Jacobean figure, possibly the courtier and writer Sir Thomas Overbury. But supporters say the case rests on more than facial resemblance: it combines family provenance, dating of the wooden panel, technical examination of the paint and an unusually revealing relationship with several early copies.

### A discovery prompted by a familiar face

The painting had long belonged to the Cobbe family and was not traditionally catalogued as Shakespeare. Its modern reassessment began after its owner, art conservator Alec Cobbe, visited an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery in London and saw a portrait often called the **Janssen portrait**, on loan from the Folger Shakespeare Library.

Cobbe was struck by the likeness between the Folger painting and the unidentified portrait in his family collection. The Folger work had long been associated with Shakespeare, although conservation research had shown that it had been altered over the centuries.

That observation opened a broader investigation. Researchers began comparing the Cobbe portrait not only with the Folger’s picture but also with several other versions of the same composition. The paintings shared more than a general Jacobean style. The sitter’s head, collar, costume and facial features corresponded closely enough to suggest that the works belonged to a single portrait tradition.

The key question was which version came first.

### Testing the panel and paint

Scientific examination helped establish that the Cobbe portrait was not a later attempt to manufacture a Shakespeare likeness. Specialists studied the oak panel on which it was painted, using tree-ring analysis and other forms of technical inspection to determine whether the support was consistent with an early-17th-century date.

The results placed the panel within the correct period for a portrait painted during Shakespeare’s lifetime. Researchers dated the work to about **1610**, although dendrochronology generally provides limits for when a tree could have been felled rather than the precise year a picture was painted.

Examination under X-radiography and infrared imaging also allowed specialists to look beneath the visible paint surface. Such techniques can reveal changes made during painting, later restorations and overpainting. Paint analysis and close inspection of the construction supported the view that the image was an authentic Jacobean portrait rather than an 18th- or 19th-century production.

The technical evidence did not, by itself, identify the man. It did, however, remove one major obstacle: the portrait appeared old enough to have been painted while Shakespeare was alive.

### The Folger portrait provides a crucial comparison

The Folger Shakespeare Library’s Janssen portrait became particularly important because it preserved evidence of how the image had been transformed.

The Folger picture had been presented as Shakespeare, but technical examination showed that later hands had changed the sitter’s appearance. Among other alterations, the hairline had been raised, making the subject look more bald and therefore more like familiar posthumous representations of Shakespeare, especially the engraved portrait by Martin Droeshout published in the 1623 First Folio.

When conservators and researchers examined the earlier layers beneath those alterations, the original form of the Folger portrait proved much closer to the Cobbe image. The fuller hair, shape of the head and arrangement of the costume indicated that the Folger work had begun as a copy of essentially the same composition before it was modified to conform to later expectations of Shakespeare’s appearance.

Digital overlays and measurements strengthened that conclusion. Details lined up so closely that researchers argued the Folger painting and other versions were not independent likenesses of similar-looking men. They were copies derived from a common prototype.

The Cobbe portrait appeared to be the strongest candidate for that prototype. Its handling was judged more immediate and accomplished than that of the copies, and it retained details that seemed to have been simplified or misunderstood in the later versions. In that reconstruction, the sequence ran from the Cobbe portrait to copies such as the Folger painting, followed by later alterations intended to make some copies look more recognizably Shakespearean.

This distinction mattered. The existence of copies labelled or accepted as Shakespeare suggested that the original composition had once carried an identification with the playwright—even if that identification later became obscured or distorted.

### Provenance adds to the case

Supporters also point to the Cobbe family’s historical connections.

The portrait descended in a collection associated with **Henry Wriothesley, the third Earl of Southampton**, Shakespeare’s patron and the dedicatee of the narrative poems *Venus and Adonis* and *The Rape of Lucrece*. The Cobbe family inherited pictures through a line connected with Southampton’s descendants.

That provenance does not prove the sitter’s identity. Old family collections can accumulate mistaken labels, and paintings can be moved, sold or misidentified. Still, the presence of the portrait in a collection linked to Southampton gives a plausible explanation for why a lifetime portrait of Shakespeare might have been preserved there.

Researchers also noted the Latin inscription at the top of the painting, taken from the classical writer Horace. It can be translated approximately as: **“How much better is this than with learning to hold the leadership of petty men.”** The inscription appears to praise the sitter as a man distinguished by intellect or literary achievement, a description compatible with Shakespeare but not exclusive to him.

### Comparison with accepted Shakespeare images

Any proposed portrait of Shakespeare must also be tested against the two likenesses generally considered to have the strongest claims to authenticity: the Droeshout engraving in the First Folio and the funerary monument in Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon.

Both were produced after Shakespeare’s death, but they were approved or commissioned by people who had known him. Researchers supporting the Cobbe identification say the portrait shares significant features with the Droeshout engraving, including the shape of the eyes, the long nose, the moustache and beard, and the proportions of the forehead and face.

The match is not exact. Painted portraits could flatter their subjects, copied images could drift from their originals, and the Droeshout engraving has often been criticized as stiff or anatomically awkward. Nevertheless, advocates argue that the similarities are stronger than would be expected by chance.

### A persuasive case, but not a settled verdict

The scientific tests can date materials, reveal hidden paint and establish relationships among copies. They cannot attach a name to a face.

That limitation remains at the heart of the debate. Critics have argued that the portrait tradition may depict another prominent man of the period. Sir Thomas Overbury has been suggested because versions of the image have been linked to his name, and because he, too, was a literary figure whose portrait might have circulated.

Skeptics also caution that labels on copies may have been added long after the sitter’s death. A later inscription identifying a painting as Shakespeare could show only that an owner believed it was Shakespeare, not that the identification was correct.

For that reason, museums and scholars generally describe the Cobbe work cautiously—as a **possible**, **probable** or **claimed** lifetime portrait rather than an unquestionably authenticated likeness.

Even with those reservations, the investigation changed the status of the painting. Before the study, it was an unidentified Jacobean portrait in a private collection. After panel dating, technical imaging, provenance research and comparison with the Folger’s altered copy, it became a serious candidate in the long search for Shakespeare’s face.

The Folger portrait was essential to that transformation. Its hidden earlier state acted like a visual record of transmission, showing how one image had been copied and then reshaped to fit the Shakespeare known from the First Folio. The Cobbe painting, apparently earlier and less altered, offered a possible source for that chain.

The result is not a scientific identification in the sense of a fingerprint or DNA match. It is a cumulative historical argument: the painting is from the right period; it came through a collection connected with Shakespeare’s patron; it appears to be the original behind several copies; at least one of those copies was associated with Shakespeare; and the face resembles accepted posthumous images.

Together, those findings have made the Cobbe portrait one of the most compelling—and most debated—possible views of William Shakespeare as his contemporaries may have seen him.

## Shakespeare with Hair: The Cobbe Portrait Reimagines the Bard

For centuries, William Shakespeare has stared back at readers with the high, domed forehead and thinning hair made familiar by the engraving in the 1623 First Folio. Martin Droeshout’s stiff, mask-like likeness—published seven years after Shakespeare’s death—helped fix the playwright in the public imagination as an already ageing genius: bald, grave and remote.

The portrait preserved in the Cobbe family collection presents a strikingly different man. Here Shakespeare—or the sitter believed by some scholars to be Shakespeare—has a full head of auburn-brown hair, a neatly trimmed beard, an elaborate lace collar and the composed bearing of a prosperous Jacobean gentleman. Rather than an abstract national monument, he appears alert, fashionable and vividly alive.

The painting came to wider public attention in 2009 after its owner, Alec Cobbe, noticed its resemblance to a portrait identified as Shakespeare at the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington. The Cobbe work, dated to around 1610, was subsequently proposed as the source for several later copies. If that identification is correct, it was painted when Shakespeare was about 46 and still living—making it a rare, perhaps unique, direct record of his appearance.

The Shakespeare scholar Stanley Wells gave the attribution its most prominent endorsement. He described the Cobbe portrait as “the only known painting of Shakespeare done from life,” while also presenting the case in terms of probability rather than absolute certainty. For Wells, the combination of the picture’s date, provenance and relationship to later images offered compelling evidence that its elegant sitter was the playwright.

The claim remains contested. Portrait attribution is an art of accumulation: family history, costume, dating, inscriptions, technical examination and resemblance must all support one another. None, on its own, can make a face speak its name. Some scholars have suggested that the sitter may instead be another well-connected Elizabethan or Jacobean figure, including the courtier Sir Thomas Overbury.

Shakespeare himself supplied an apt warning against overconfidence. In *Macbeth*, after hearing of the treachery of the former Thane of Cawdor, King Duncan observes:

> “There’s no art  
> To find the mind’s construction in the face.”

The line concerns moral character, not portrait identification, but it resonates uncannily with the debate. A face can invite intimacy while withholding proof. Viewers may search the Cobbe sitter’s eyes for wit, theatrical intelligence or authorial self-possession, yet those qualities may reveal as much about Shakespeare’s cultural afterlife as about the man before the painter.

That is part of the portrait’s fascination. The familiar Droeshout image asks us to accept Shakespeare as an icon. The Cobbe portrait allows us to imagine him as a contemporary: ambitious, socially assured and still in possession of his hair. Whether it is ultimately judged an authentic likeness or an alluring Jacobean near-miss, it unsettles the bald, monumental Bard—and reminds us how strongly we want genius to have a recognizable face.
